analysis.one_liner: Bans grossly excessive prices for food, fuel, and medical essentials during declared emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2025 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Defense Production Act to bar sellers from charging prices that grossly exceed what they charged before a declared shortage. It covers consumer food, essential medical supplies, fuel, electricity, and home heating oil, and it defines a shortage broadly — including natural disasters, pandemics, supply-chain disruptions, and extreme industry consolidation. A price jump of 10 percent or more would be presumed excessive unless the seller shows it reflects a legitimate business need or higher costs beyond its control, and violators could be fined up to three times the revenue gained.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that depend on groceries, home heating, gasoline, and medical supplies — that is, essentially everyone — would gain protection from sudden price spikes when emergencies or supply disruptions hit. Ordinary sellers who keep prices steady would also benefit from a clearer rule of the road against competitors who raise prices sharply during a crisis.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households buying food, fuel, and medicine

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a federal offense to sell covered goods at prices that grossly exceed pre-shortage levels, with a 10 percent price increase creating a presumption of an 'unfairly excessive price.' [S2] [S1] [S3] [S4] [S5] [S6] [S7] [S8]
It covers the necessities households cannot go without during a crisis: consumer food, essential medical and emergency supplies and services, fuel, electricity, and home heating oil. [S2]
The penalty is steep — the greater of $20,000 or 300 percent of the revenue generated in violation — which gives sellers a concrete financial reason not to exploit a shortage. [S2]

It recognizes 'extreme industry consolidation' itself as a cause of an acute shortage, aiming the rule at markets where a few dominant sellers can raise prices with little competition to stop them. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Sellers of covered goods — grocery and food retailers, fuel and electricity providers, home heating oil dealers, and medical suppliers — would bear the cost: potential fines of up to triple the revenue from any price deemed unfairly excessive, plus the burden of documenting that price changes reflect legitimate costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sellers of food, fuel, and medical supplies

drawbacks.text: A presumptive threshold of a 10 percent price increase is low; it could capture ordinary price adjustments by businesses with thin margins, though the bill exempts increases that reflect a legitimate business need or costs outside the seller's control. [S2]

The standard economic objection to emergency price limits is that they can backfire: if sellers cannot raise prices, they have less incentive to restock scarce goods quickly or conserve supply, which can deepen the shortage the rule is meant to ease.

The definition of 'acute shortage' is broad — it includes any 'similar exigent constraint' — which could invite disputes over when the prohibition applies and how 'prevailing market prices' are measured. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households facing a natural disaster, pandemic, or fuel disruption, protection against sudden price spikes is a real and immediate benefit, and the bill's carve-outs for legitimate cost increases blunt the main fairness objection. The genuine trade-off is the classic one in shortage economics: capping prices may slow the restocking that ends a shortage. On balance the bill is a consumer-protection measure with a defensible design, not a radical intervention — it only applies during declared or acute shortages and builds in seller defenses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee when introduced, and the committee has taken no further action on it; Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Josh Riley of New York introduced the bill on July 23, 2025. [S1] [S4]
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day. [S4] [S1]
No other action has been taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no cosponsors have joined. [S4] [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the outcome is simply inaction: sellers of food, fuel, and medical supplies remain unregulated at the federal level against emergency price spikes, and no interest has had to change its behavior because the bill has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sellers of essentials, untouched by new rules

for.name: Rep. Josh Riley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its only sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has no cosponsors from either party and has never had a vote, so no partisan split on the merits can be measured; it currently rests entirely with its one Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would expose them to fines of up to three times the revenue from prices judged unfairly excessive during acute shortages. Their interest in charging market-clearing prices runs against households' interest in stable prices for necessities.

industries.industry: Fuel, electricity, and home heating oil providers
industries.note: Energy resources are explicitly covered, so utilities and fuel sellers could not raise prices more than modestly during a declared or acute shortage without facing penalties. Households that must heat their homes and fill their tanks are the intended beneficiaries.

Essential medical and emergency supplies and services are covered goods, restricting price spikes during disease outbreaks, disasters, or other emergencies. Their interest in crisis pricing runs against patients' interest in affordable care and supplies.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action since its July 2025 referral, the bill is highly unlikely to advance in this Congress; the typical path for a bill at this stage is to remain in committee until the session ends.
